title: Nutrition and Common Chronic Diseases

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a chronic disease as a houseguest who moves in and stays for years, not a cold that visits for a weekend. Because it sticks around, the everyday choices you make, especially what you eat, really shape how it behaves over time. That slow, long-term nature is exactly what the word chronic means.

### Question 2

Salt acts like a sponge in your blood, pulling in extra water. More water in the pipes means more pressure pushing on the walls, just like a garden hose swells when you crank the tap. That is why cutting back on sodium helps keep blood pressure down.

### Question 3

Not all fats behave the same way. Saturated and trans fats push up the amount of "bad" LDL cholesterol floating in your blood, and it is that extra LDL working its way into artery walls that slowly builds plaque. Unsaturated fats from things like fish, nuts, and olive oil nudge that number down instead, so trading them in helps keep your blood highways clearer.

### Question 4

Bile is a digestive juice your body builds out of cholesterol. Soluble fiber grabs that bile like a sticky net and drags it out of your body. To make more bile, your liver has to pull cholesterol out of your blood, so your cholesterol level drops.

### Question 5

Insulin is the key that lets sugar into your cells. In type 1, the body can't make the key at all. In type 2, the body makes keys but the locks get rusty and stop working well, and that rustiness is often tied to weight and eating habits.

### Question 6

Sugar by itself races into your blood like water down a slide. Fiber, protein, and fat act like speed bumps that slow the sugar down, so it trickles in instead of flooding in. A steadier flow is much easier for the body to handle.

### Question 7

DASH is like a recipe for calmer blood pressure. It loads your plate with fruits, veggies, whole grains, and low-fat dairy, which are full of minerals that relax blood vessels, and it dials back the salt that raises pressure. The whole point is a gentler push on your artery walls.

### Question 8

Foods packed with added sugar and stripped-down grains give you a quick flood of energy but not much staying power, so you tend to eat more and store the extra. Over time that pattern wears out the body's sugar-handling system, which is how type 2 diabetes and weight gain creep in.

### Question 9

Brown rice keeps its outer coat, which is full of fiber, while white rice has that coat polished off. Keeping the coat means more fiber to slow digestion and help your heart. The other swaps go the wrong way, trading good foods for greasier or emptier ones.

### Question 10

If sodium is the bully that raises your blood pressure, potassium is the helper that shows sodium the door and tells your blood vessels to relax. Both actions take pressure off your artery walls, which is why potassium-rich foods are so useful for high blood pressure.

### Question 11

Eating mostly plants, whole grains, and fish while going easy on processed meat and sugar is like giving your body high-quality fuel year after year. That steady care lowers the odds of several big diseases at once. But it can't stop type 1 diabetes, because that one comes from the immune system, not the plate.

### Question 12

Picture your bones as a vault of calcium, with vitamin D acting as the guard who unlocks the door so calcium can get inside. Keep both well stocked and the vault stays strong, which is how you fend off the brittle bones of osteoporosis. The other pairings flip the roles around, so they simply don't hold up.
